'''Robert Balson Dingle''' (26 March 1926 – 2 March 2010) was a British theoretical physicist.

==Education==
Dingle studied at the [[University of Cambridge]], UK (Tripos Part I 1945, Part II 1946).  He spent the year 1947-1948 at the [[University of Bristol]] where he worked under the supervision of Professors [[Nevill Francis Mott]] and [[Herbert Fröhlich]], and then continued research in [[theoretical physics]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] under the supervision of Professor [[Douglas Hartree]], earning the Ph.D. there in 1952.  Following research positions in Delft (Netherlands) and in Ottawa (Canada) he was appointed Reader in [[theoretical physics]] at the [[University of Western Australia]] in Perth. In June 1960 he was appointed as the first occupant of the Chair of [[Theoretical Physics]] at the [[University of St. Andrews]], UK.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Theoretical Physics at St. Andrews: Prof. R.B. Dingle | magazine=Nature | date=13 February 1960 | page=430}}</ref> In 1961 he was elected as a [[Fellowship of the Royal Society of Edinburgh|fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (FRSE)]].{{fact|date=August 2025}}

In later years he spent sabbatical periods in Canada, California and in Australia, and through ill-health he retired in 1987.<ref name="rseobit">{{cite web |title=Robert Balson Dingle obituary |url=https://rse.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Image-and-Obituary_Michael-Berry-John-Cornwell_undated.pdf |website=rse.org.uk |accessdate=24 February 2026}}</ref>

==Research areas==
Dingle’s research areas in [[theoretical physics]] were [[condensed matter physics]] and [[statistical mechanics]]; in particular he made significant original contributions in [[Bose–Einstein statistics|Bose-Einstein]] statistics of particles with special reference to low temperatures,<ref>R.B. Dingle, Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 45 (1949) 275-287</ref> magnetic and surface properties of metals,<ref>R.B. Dingle, Physica 19 (1953) 311, 729</ref> the anomalous [[skin effect]] in anisotropic metals and  semiconductors,<ref>R.B. Dingle, Physica 22 (1956) 1237; Proc. Roy. Soc. A224 (1954) 260, 273</ref> and liquid helium II.<ref>R.B. Dingle, Adv. Phys. 1 (1952) 111-168</ref>   In [[mathematical physics]] he made major contributions in the fields of [[Bose–Einstein integral|Bose-Einstein]] integrals,<ref>R.B. Dingle, Appl. Sci. Res. B4 (1955) 401, B6 (1957) 240-244</ref><ref>R.B. Dingle, Appl. Sci. Res. B6 (1957) 144</ref> [[Fermi–Dirac statistics|Fermi-Dirac]] integrals,<ref>R.B. Dingle, Appl. Sci. Res. B6 (1957) 225-239</ref> and  [[Mathieu functions]].<ref>R.B. Dingle and H.J. W. Müller, J. reine angew. Math. 211 (1962)11-32; 216 (1964) 123-133</ref> A main research area of Dingle's was the subject of asymptotic expansions with regard to their derivation and interpretation.<ref>R.B. Dingle, Proc. Roy. Soc. A244 (1958) 456, 476, 484; A349 (1959) 270, 285, 293.</ref> His extensive researches in this latter field he compiled in his monograph on [[asymptotic expansions]].<ref>{{Cite book|isbn=0122165500|title=Asymptotic Expansions: Their Derivation and Interpretation|last1=Dingle|first1=Robert B.|year=1973}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=Asymptotic Expansions: Their Derivation and Interpretation | url=https://michaelberryphysics.files.wordpress.com/2013/07/dingle.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170807202513/https://michaelberryphysics.files.wordpress.com/2013/07/dingle.pdf | archive-date=2017-08-07}}</ref>
